title: Hydrocarbons: addition, radical chains and aromatic reactions
subject: Chemistry

chapters.title: Frameworks, formulas and unsaturation
chapters.script: Welcome to Hydrocarbons. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen. Start with connectivity before choosing a reaction. An acyclic saturated alkane has two more hydrogen atoms than twice its carbon count. One ring or one double bond removes two hydrogens relative to that saturated reference; one triple bond removes four. The degree of unsaturation counts rings and pi bonds. For a neutral ordinary hydrocarbon, take twice the carbon count plus two, subtract the hydrogen count, and divide by two. Benzene's formula gives four, consistent with one ring and three pi bonds in a conventional contributor. The formula alone does not prove benzene: other connectivities can share it. Butane has zero degrees, butene has one, and butyne has two. In but two ene, each double bonded carbon carries two different groups, permitting geometrical isomers. A terminal double bond with two hydrogens on one carbon does not meet that requirement. Check valence, hydrogen count and possible stereoisomers before interpreting a formula as one unique molecule.

chapters.title: Conformations and radical chains
chapters.script: Rotation about ethane's carbon carbon single bond changes its conformation without changing which atoms are connected. In a Newman view along that bond, an eclipsed arrangement aligns front and back bonds, while a staggered arrangement offsets them. Staggered ethane has lower energy in the introductory model. These are conformations, not different constitutional isomers. Alkane chlorination under light changes connectivity through a radical chain. Initiation breaks a chlorine molecule homolytically to form two chlorine radicals. In propagation, a chlorine radical removes hydrogen from methane to give hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical. That methyl radical reacts with another chlorine molecule to form chloromethane and regenerate a chlorine radical. Each propagation sequence therefore maintains a reactive radical. Termination joins two radicals without generating another. Repeated substitution can form products beyond the first chlorinated compound, and unsymmetrical alkanes can give several positions of substitution. Product amounts depend on both how many hydrogens are available and their relative reaction rates. Do not predict product percentages from radical stability alone or assume all halogenations have identical selectivity.
points: Propagation · CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• · Radical regenerated
Termination · CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl · Radicals consumed

chapters.title: Alkene orientation depends on pathway
chapters.formula: Propene + HBr: ionic and peroxide pathways differ
chapters.script: An alkene's pi electrons can begin bonding to an electrophile. In ordinary ionic addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, protonation can lead toward a secondary or a primary carbocation. The pathway involving the more stable secondary intermediate is favoured, and bromide capture gives mainly two bromopropane. This is the familiar Markovnikov orientation for this substrate and these conditions. It is a result of a mechanism, not a direction rule independent of reagents. Carbocation rearrangements can change products in substrates where a more favourable intermediate is accessible. Suitable peroxide initiated radical conditions change the hydrogen bromide pathway. Bromine radical addition that forms the more stable carbon radical leads, after hydrogen abstraction, mainly to one bromopropane. The standard peroxide reversal applies to hydrogen bromide; it must not be transferred automatically to hydrogen chloride or hydrogen iodide. For every prediction write the alkene, reagent and radical or ionic conditions together. The carbon skeleton has three carbons in both propene products; the location of bromine changes, while no carbon is gained or lost.
points: HCl or HI + peroxides · No general HBr shortcut · Check actual chemistry

chapters.title: Hydrogenation, halogenation and hydration
chapters.formula: The solvent and catalyst help define the reaction
chapters.script: Adding hydrogen to an alkene with an appropriate metal catalyst converts its double bond into a single bond. Ethene becomes ethane, consuming one mole of hydrogen per mole of double bonds. Alkene bromination in a suitable non-nucleophilic medium commonly forms a vicinal dibromide, with bromine atoms on adjacent carbons. A bridged intermediate explains the usual anti addition rather than a freely rotating carbocation picture. If water is present, it can compete as a nucleophile and change the product toward a bromohydrin. Therefore a reagent name without solvent information may not fully specify the chemistry. Acid catalysed hydration of propene gives mainly propan two ol through the usual ionic orientation. Simply mixing an alkene with water does not imply rapid hydration without suitable conditions. In addition polymerization, many ethene molecules join as the pi bonds are replaced by bonds along a saturated chain. The polyethene repeat unit contains two carbon atoms each bearing two hydrogens. Distinguish a repeat unit from a whole polymer molecule.
points: Alkene · Br₂; non-nucleophilic medium · Vicinal dibromide

chapters.title: Ozonolysis reconstructs double bonds
chapters.script: Ozonolysis is useful for locating an alkene double bond when the work-up is specified. Under reductive work-up, split the double bond and convert each of its carbons into a carbonyl carbon. Keep the other groups attached to that carbon. For but two ene, each double bonded carbon carries hydrogen and methyl, so each fragment is acetaldehyde, a two carbon aldehyde. One original molecule gives two acetaldehyde molecules. This result identifies the connectivity but does not by itself distinguish the geometrical isomers of but two ene. For two methylpropene, one double bonded carbon bears two methyl groups and gives propanone; the terminal carbon bears two hydrogens and gives formaldehyde, a one carbon aldehyde. Add the fragment carbon counts: three plus one returns the original four. A double bonded carbon with no hydrogen commonly yields a ketone fragment. A carbon bearing hydrogen can yield an aldehyde under the stated reductive conditions. Oxidative work-up can further change aldehyde products, so it must not be treated as interchangeable. Work backward by reconnecting the two carbonyl carbons when reconstructing a possible alkene.
points: Each C=C carbon · Becomes carbonyl C · Keep attached groups

chapters.title: Alkynes: acidity and selective reduction
chapters.formula: Terminal sp C–H differs from an ordinary alkane C–H
chapters.script: A terminal alkyne has hydrogen directly attached to a carbon of the triple bond. Removing this hydrogen gives an acetylide ion. The greater s character of an sp orbital stabilizes the negative charge compared with comparable simple sp two or sp three carbanions. Terminal alkynes are consequently more acidic than comparable alkenes and alkanes, while remaining much weaker acids than water. A sufficiently strong base such as sodium amide can form an acetylide; aqueous hydroxide is not a quantitative substitute. Acetylides can form carbon carbon bonds with suitable unhindered primary alkyl halides by substitution, while more hindered substrates can favour elimination. Complete catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne consumes two equivalents of hydrogen to reach an alkane. Selective partial hydrogenation with a Lindlar catalyst can give a cis alkene from an appropriate internal alkyne. Dissolving metal reduction can instead give the trans alkene. The alkene formed from a terminal triple bond has a carbon bearing two hydrogens, so cis and trans labels do not apply. Reagents and equivalents decide how far the reduction proceeds.
points: Internal alkyne · H₂; Lindlar catalyst · Cis alkene
Internal alkyne · Dissolving metal reduction · Trans alkene

chapters.title: Aromaticity and aromatic substitution
chapters.formula: Planar cyclic conjugation plus 4n + 2 π electrons
chapters.script: Benzene is a planar cyclic conjugated system with six pi electrons. It satisfies the introductory four n plus two aromatic electron rule with n equal to one. Electron count alone is insufficient: a molecule must also have the required cyclic conjugation and appropriate geometry. Benzene's carbon carbon bonds are equivalent; alternating bond drawings are contributors to a delocalized structure. In common electrophilic aromatic substitution, the ring forms a new bond to an electrophile and temporarily loses aromaticity. Removal of a proton restores the conjugated ring. Bromination commonly uses bromine with a Lewis acid such as iron three bromide. Nitration uses conditions that generate the nitronium electrophile. These ring substitutions replace a ring hydrogen and retain the six carbon framework. They differ from radical substitution on an alkyl side chain under light. In toluene, identify whether conditions target the aromatic ring or the benzylic position before assigning a product. Treat aromatic stabilization as an explanation for common reaction preferences, rather than a claim that an aromatic ring can never undergo any addition reaction.
points: Bromination · Br₂ with FeBr₃ · Ring H replaced
Side-chain halogenation · Radical conditions · Different reaction site

chapters.title: Directing groups and synthesis checks
chapters.formula: Activation and directing position are separate questions
chapters.script: A substituent influences both how rapidly an aromatic ring reacts and where a new group is introduced. An alkyl group generally activates the ring and favours ortho and para substitution. A nitro group deactivates the ring and favours meta substitution. Halogens are an important mixed case: they deactivate overall through electron withdrawal but direct toward ortho and para positions through resonance donation. A directing preference does not promise one pure positional product. Friedel Crafts alkylation introduces an alkyl group under suitable Lewis acid conditions, but rearrangements and repeated alkylation can complicate the result. Acylation introduces an acyl group and avoids the analogous carbocation skeleton rearrangement. Strongly deactivated rings and catalyst binding groups can prevent the usual reaction, so do not apply the name without checking the substrate. In a short synthesis, mark the reaction centre, count carbons, state the reagent and inspect competing pathways at each arrow. Use the practice questions to connect these choices rather than memorizing product names alone. More preparation routes and detailed stereochemical drawings remain useful.

chapters.title: Alkyne hydration gives carbonyl products
chapters.formula: Propyne: Hg²⁺/acid hydration → propanone; hydroboration–oxidation → propanal
chapters.script: Alkyne hydration usually requires following an initially formed enol to its carbonyl tautomer. An enol has hydroxyl attached to an alkene carbon; the final carbonyl product is not obtained by simply leaving that double bond unchanged. For propyne, aqueous acid with mercury two catalysis gives the Markovnikov hydration pattern and, after tautomerization, propanone. A suitable bulky borane followed by alkaline peroxide oxidation instead gives the terminal alkyne the complementary hydration orientation, leading to the aldehyde C H three, C H two, C H O, also called propionaldehyde. Both products retain the three carbon skeleton. They have the same molecular formula but different carbonyl positions and functional classes. Ethyne is an important special case: its acid catalysed hydration gives the aldehyde C H three, C H O, also called acetaldehyde, rather than a methyl ketone. Internal unsymmetrical alkynes can give product mixtures, so a terminal alkyne shortcut must not be applied indiscriminately. Read the catalyst and workup before selecting a product. Tautomerization moves a proton and changes bond placement; it is not merely resonance between drawings with the same hydrogen attachments. This distinction connects hydrocarbon reactions with the carbonyl chemistry developed in the Organic Oxygen class.

chapters.title: Reconstruct an alkene from carbonyl fragments
chapters.formula: Reductive ozonolysis: join the two carbonyl carbons with C=C
chapters.script: Reductive ozonolysis can be read backward as well as forward. Each carbon of the original double bond becomes a carbonyl carbon while retaining its attached carbon groups. Suppose the products are one molecule of propanone and one of acetaldehyde, the two carbon aldehyde C H three, C H O. Propanone's carbonyl carbon carries two methyl groups. This aldehyde's carbonyl carbon carries one methyl group and one hydrogen. Join those two carbonyl carbons with a double bond and remove the carbonyl oxygens in the reconstruction. The original alkene is two methylbut two ene. It contains five carbons, matching three plus two in the products. This reconstruction determines connectivity, but carbonyl fragments alone do not generally recover an alkene's original E or Z geometry. In this particular alkene, two identical methyl groups on one double bonded carbon prevent E and Z isomerism. The workup matters: oxidative ozonolysis can further oxidize aldehyde products, changing the evidence used for reconstruction. State reductive conditions before treating an aldehyde as the final fragment. Finish by counting carbon atoms and checking which double bonded carbon had a hydrogen.

chapters.title: Check aromaticity before counting alone
chapters.formula: Cyclic, planar, continuously conjugated; 4n + 2 π electrons
chapters.script: Aromaticity in the simple Hückel model requires more than a special electron count. The ring must be cyclic, approximately planar and continuously conjugated, with a suitable p orbital at each position. A closed shell ring with four n plus two pi electrons can then be aromatic. Benzene has six pi electrons, corresponding to n equal to one. The cyclopentadienyl anion also has six: four from two double bonds and two from the relevant lone pair in its conjugated ring. The cycloheptatrienyl cation has six pi electrons from three double bonds and an empty p orbital at the cationic position. Charge alone therefore does not prohibit aromaticity. A planar fully conjugated four pi electron ring instead fits the antiaromatic pattern. A nonplanar molecule that avoids continuous effective overlap may be nonaromatic rather than antiaromatic, even if a naive count gives four n electrons. Cyclooctatetraene is the familiar nonplanar example. Always check geometry and conjugation before applying the electron rule. The model here concerns simple monocyclic systems and is not a universal classification shortcut for every fused or unusual structure.
points: Benzene · Planar conjugated ring · 6 π; aromatic
Cyclopentadienyl anion · Lone pair participates · 6 π; aromatic

chapters.title: Separate directing effects from activation
chapters.formula: Halogens: deactivating yet ortho/para-directing in electrophilic substitution
chapters.script: An existing substituent affects both how fast an aromatic ring reacts and where a new group preferentially enters. Those are separate questions. Relative to carbon one bearing the substituent, carbons two and six are ortho, three and five are meta, and carbon four is para. A methyl group commonly activates the ring toward electrophilic substitution and favours ortho and para products. A nitro group strongly deactivates and favours meta substitution. Halogens are the important combination: they deactivate the ring overall but still direct predominantly ortho and para. Their inductive withdrawal and resonance donation influence different aspects of the comparison. Do not infer that an ortho para director must always make the ring more reactive than benzene. Nor does directing preference promise one pure product. Steric effects, electrophile, medium and additional substituents can affect the product mixture. The labelled rings show relative positions rather than exact yields. For several substituents, compare their competing effects and blocked sites before predicting the next position. Keep electrophilic ring substitution distinct from radical reaction at an alkyl side chain.
points: Methyl substituent · Electrophilic substitution · Activating; ortho/para
Nitro substituent · Electrophilic substitution · Deactivating; meta
Halogen substituent · Electrophilic substitution · Deactivating; ortho/para

chapters.title: Benzylic reactions need the right site
chapters.formula: Side-chain oxidation usually requires at least one benzylic H
chapters.script: The benzylic carbon is directly attached to an aromatic ring. Its chemistry differs from that of a carbon bearing hydrogen within the ring itself. Under the usual strong side chain oxidation conditions, an alkylbenzene with at least one benzylic hydrogen can yield a carboxyl group at the ring attachment, followed by acid workup. Toluene and ethylbenzene therefore both give benzoic acid in that introductory comparison. The extra carbon in ethylbenzene does not become a longer carboxylic acid side chain. Carbon lost from the side chain must be accounted for in a full balanced oxidation, rather than silently assumed to remain in the main organic product. Tert butylbenzene has no hydrogen on its benzylic carbon and does not follow this ordinary side chain oxidation shortcut. Radical halogenation under suitable light or radical initiating conditions can also target benzylic positions, whereas electrophilic aromatic halogenation uses a different pathway and catalyst context. Identify the reacting carbon, the presence of its hydrogen and the reagent conditions before deciding whether the ring or side chain changes.
points: Toluene · Benzylic H present · Benzoic acid after workup
Ethylbenzene · Benzylic H present · Benzoic acid after workup
tert-Butylbenzene · No benzylic H · Shortcut does not apply

quiz.question: Ordinary ionic addition of HBr to propene mainly gives:
quiz.explanation: The favoured secondary carbocation pathway places bromine at the middle carbon.

quiz.question: The familiar peroxide-induced reversed HX orientation applies to:
quiz.explanation: The standard peroxide effect is associated with HBr, not a general rule for all hydrogen halides.

quiz.question: Reductive ozonolysis of but-2-ene gives:
quiz.explanation: Each double-bond carbon retains its H and CH3 substituents and becomes an ethanal carbonyl carbon.

quiz.question: The lower-energy ethane conformation in the elementary model is:
quiz.explanation: Staggered ethane has less torsional strain than the eclipsed arrangement.

quiz.question: A chlorine substituent on benzene is generally:
quiz.explanation: Halogens withdraw inductively and deactivate, while resonance donation favours ortho/para substitution.

quiz.question: Which hydrocarbon has hydrogen directly attached to an sp carbon?
quiz.explanation: Ethyne is a terminal alkyne with an sp carbon-hydrogen bond, responsible for its distinctive acidity.

quiz.question: The degree of unsaturation of neutral hydrocarbon C6H6 is:
quiz.explanation: (2 × 6 + 2 − 6)/2 = 4. This count does not uniquely identify benzene.

quiz.question: Reductive ozonolysis of 2-methylpropene gives:
quiz.explanation: The carbon bearing two methyl groups gives propanone; the terminal CH2 carbon gives methanal.

quiz.question: Partial hydrogenation of an appropriate internal alkyne with a Lindlar catalyst usually gives:
quiz.explanation: The Lindlar system allows selective partial hydrogenation with the usual cis relationship for an appropriate internal alkyne.

quiz.question: Which group is generally deactivating and meta directing in aromatic substitution?
quiz.explanation: Nitro deactivates and directs meta. Chlorine deactivates but directs ortho/para.

quiz.question: Propyne under aqueous acid/Hg(II) hydration gives mainly:
quiz.explanation: The initial enol tautomerizes to propanone under the stated Markovnikov hydration conditions.

quiz.question: Propanone and ethanal from reductive ozonolysis reconstruct:
quiz.explanation: Join the carbonyl carbons: one bears two methyls and the other methyl plus H; total carbon count is five.

quiz.question: The cyclopentadienyl anion has how many π electrons in its aromatic ring?
quiz.explanation: Two double bonds contribute four and the conjugated lone pair contributes two.

quiz.question: A halogen substituent in ordinary electrophilic aromatic substitution is:
quiz.explanation: Overall inductive deactivation coexists with ortho/para directing resonance effects.

quiz.question: Which lacks a benzylic hydrogen for the ordinary alkylbenzene oxidation shortcut?
quiz.explanation: The ring-attached carbon in tert-butylbenzene is bonded to three methyl groups and has no H.

quiz.question: Propyne with suitable bulky-borane hydroboration followed by oxidation gives:
quiz.explanation: The complementary hydration orientation of this terminal alkyne gives the aldehyde propanal.
